summary: Explains why weak or predictable random number generators are a serious risk for TLS and similar security protocols, and describes a way for implementations to harden their randomness. The idea is to mix a long-term private key into the random generator's inputs, so that output stays unpredictable even if the system's entropy source is weak.

eli5.summary: Secret codes only work if nobody can guess your dice rolls. This suggests also stirring in something only you know, so even if your dice are a bit lopsided, the result stays hard to guess.

questions: why is randomness important for tls
how to improve random number generation in security protocols
subtitle: A way to mix a long-term private key into a random number generator so its output stays unpredictable even if the generator is broken.

tldr.problem: Weak, backdoored or badly seeded random number generators can let an attacker predict the secrets that TLS and similar protocols rely on.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of using raw generator output G(n), use G'(n), which hashes a signature made with the long-term private key over a fixed tag, extracts a key from it together with the generator output, and expands that key with a changing tag.
tldr.outcome: If the generator is broken but the private key stays secret, the output remains indistinguishable from random. The RFC is Informational and comes from the CFRG.

today: RFC 8937 is an Informational RFC from the Crypto Forum Research Group of the IRTF, published in October 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Weak Randomness Hurts
sections.content:
Protocols such as TLS use a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG) to create ephemeral key shares and the ClientHello and ServerHello random values. If the generator is poorly implemented, an adversary may predict its output and recover secret key material.

The RFC points to two kinds of failure. A bug, such as the Debian bug it cites, can make generators weak by accident. A generator can also be weakened on purpose, as with the Dual EC example it cites. A weak initial entropy source breaks every generator seeded from it.

The idea is inspired by the NAXOS trick, where a raw random value x is replaced by H(x, sk) for the sender's private key sk. Private keys often live in Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) that may only offer signing, so the RFC uses a signature instead.
sections.eli5: If the dice you roll for your secret code are rigged, a sneaky person can guess your code. This document is about making the dice harder to rig.

sections.title: The Randomness Wrapper
sections.content:
Let G(n) produce n random bytes from a CSPRNG. The augmented generator is:

G'(n) = Expand(Extract(H(Sig(sk, tag1)), G(L)), tag2, n)

  • Sig(sk, m) signs message m with the private key.
  • H is a cryptographic hash function.
  • Extract and Expand are a randomness extractor and a variable-length output PRF, for example HKDF-Extract and HKDF-Expand from RFC 5869.
  • tag1 is a fixed string and tag2 is a changing one, such as a counter. The RFC requires L >= n - L', where L' is the length of tag2.

The security depends on the secrecy of H(Sig(sk, tag1)) and G(L). If the signature leaks, security falls back to expanding directly from G(L).
sections.eli5: You take your normal dice roll, stir in a secret stamp only you can make, and then stretch the mix into as many random numbers as you need.

sections.title: Signatures, Tags and Cost
sections.content:
Sig(sk, tag1) needs to be computed only once and can be cached, so the extra cost compared with G(n) tends to be negligible next to protocol operations. Values of G'(n) can also be precomputed and pooled. If the key is in an HSM, only the signature has to be computed inside it.

Sig MUST be deterministic, for example deterministic ECDSA from RFC 6979, or use an independent and completely reliable entropy source such as an HSM's own. The signature MUST NOT be used or exposed beyond this computation.

The tags MUST never collide with another contender or owner of the key, which can happen when one HSM serves several servers or when virtual machines are cloned. For tag1, the RFC recommends a constant string bound to a device and protocol, including information that makes each virtual machine instance unique. For tag2, it recommends a nonce, such as a counter or a timer that differs on every invocation.
sections.eli5: The secret stamp is made once and kept. Every time you need random numbers you also add a number that never repeats, so no two batches are alike.

sections.title: Use in TLS and Implementation Guidance
sections.content:
The wrapper fits any protocol where a party has a long-term private key and generates randomness, which is true of most TLS servers. To use it in TLS, replace the private CSPRNG, the one that generates values such as key shares, with HKDF-Expand(HKDF-Extract(H(Sig(sk, tag1)), G(L)), tag2, n).

If an application needs more than the bound n <= L + L' allows, implementations can call G' several times and concatenate the results. Implementations SHOULD apply the technique when indirect access to a private key is available and CSPRNG guarantees are dubious, or when they want stronger guarantees about future issues.
sections.eli5: A web server can use this trick on the secret numbers it makes for each connection. If it needs more numbers, it just asks again and glues the answers together.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC lists three properties. If the CSPRNG works, the output is also indistinguishable from random. An adversary controlling a broken CSPRNG and seeing all outputs does not gain a non-negligible advantage in leaking the private key, absent side-channel attacks. If the CSPRNG is broken, the output stays indistinguishable from random while the private key remains unknown.

A security analysis was performed in the paper it cites as SecAnalysis. A signature that uses weak entropy defeats the construction through repeat-randomness attacks, which is why Sig must be deterministic or use a reliable independent source. A side-channel attack is the main way the signature might be exposed, so the RFC recommends generating a key just for this construction.

The construction cannot give guarantees if the CSPRNG state is cloned through virtual machine snapshots or process forking, so tag1 should include all available information about the environment.
sections.eli5: Even with broken dice, your secret stamp keeps the numbers safe, as long as the stamp stays secret and you do not copy the whole machine.

sections.title: Comparison to RFC 6979
sections.content:
Both this construction and RFC 6979 use private keys to seed a deterministic generator. RFC 6979 recommends instantiating HMAC_DRBG with the private key as the entropy input and H(m) as the nonce. Here, a key derived from G(n) and H(Sig(sk, tag1)) is the entropy input and tag2 is the nonce.

The goals differ. This construction keeps trusted randomness even if the CSPRNG is completely broken. RFC 6979 does not assume any entropy source at all. Inside an HSM, RFC 6979 would run in the HSM for signing, while this wrapper calls the HSM's signature.
sections.eli5: Another recipe also uses a secret key to make numbers, but it is for making signatures when you have no dice at all. This one is for fixing bad dice.
